scripts.opening:opening:
[measured] Architects of Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] An autumn afternoon on Prairie Avenue, 1904, the low sun raking across stone. [short pause] Thirty-three years ago Chicago burned; it rebuilt itself as a daring new city, and many of the architects who did it built houses on this street, for clients who could pay for anything.

[short pause] Seven houses on foot, 1701 to 2100 Prairie: the man who built the first skyscraper, a giant from Boston, the firm of Cobb and Frost, the young Burnham and Root, the designer of a whole company town, the architect of the Statue of Liberty's pedestal, and the house that started it all for Daniel Burnham. [short pause] He married the client's daughter.

[short pause] Begin at 1701, with a modest Italianate front by a very immodest engineer.
scripts.stop:jenney: [measured] 1701 Prairie, William G. Hibbard's house of 1869, for the president of a big wholesale hardware firm. [short pause] Its architect, William Le Baron Jenney, trained as an engineer, and fifteen years after this house he built the Home Insurance Building downtown: 'The building was the first fully metal-framed building and is considered the first skyscraper'. [short pause] His drafting room was the school of a generation: Louis Sullivan, Daniel Burnham, William Holabird and Martin Roche 'performed their architectural apprenticeships on Jenney's staff'. Here he gave Hibbard a sober Italianate, a low hipped roof on bracketed eaves. [short pause] The house will end with a fitting tenant: from 1921 its owners give Sullivan a free office here until his death in 1924, and in 1932 it is razed. [short pause] South to the corner, and a very different kind of genius.
scripts.stop:richardson: [measured] 1800 Prairie, Henry Hobson Richardson's house for John J. Glessner. [short pause] Glessner remembered his architect weighing 370 pounds: 'big-minded, big-bodied, big-hearted'. [short pause] Three weeks before he died, too ill to leave his bedroom, Richardson marked where the lights would go and said, 'There, Mr. Glessner if I were to live five years longer, that is the last thing I would do on your house, my part is finished.' [short pause] He died on 26 April 1886; building began on 1 June, and Norcross Brothers built it for the contract price, not a dollar more. The neighbours were appalled. George Pullman grumbled about 'that thing staring me in the face'. [short pause] Now look next door.
scripts.stop:cobb-frost: [measured] 1808 Prairie, next door, by Cobb and Frost for Osborn R. Keith. [short pause] The notice of 1886 reads like a price tag: a three-storey dwelling, 38 by 80 feet, with a granite front, at a cost of forty thousand dollars. [short pause] This house went up the same year Richardson's drawings next door were being built, granite answering granite. When it is razed in 1968, its north wall will be left standing to keep the Glessner courtyard private. [short pause] Two doors south is the firm that would outbuild them all.
scripts.stop:burnham-root: [measured] 1812 Prairie, George H. Wheeler's house of 1884 by Burnham and Root: a picturesque brick row house in the Dutch manner, its front carried up as a tall shaped gable over a stone first storey. [short pause] It will be razed in 1968. Within a decade Burnham would run the building of the 1893 World's Fair, the 'White City'. His motto: 'Make no little plans. [short pause] They have no magic to stir men's blood and probably will not themselves be realized.' [short pause] Cross the avenue to a chateau by a man who once planned an entire town.
scripts.stop:beman: [measured] 1801 Prairie, Solon S. Beman's chateau of 1890 for the piano maker William W. Kimball, French Chateauesque, steep slate and a round tower. [short pause] Beman was in his twenties when he 'received a commission from George Pullman to design what would become the nation's first planned company town', Pullman, south of the city. [short pause] He also added the palm room and conservatory to Pullman's own house up the street. [short pause] Walk south to the street's most famous name, and the most famous architect.
scripts.stop:hunt: [measured] 1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's house, by Richard Morris Hunt of New York. [short pause] 'Hunt was the first American to be admitted to the school of architecture at the École des Beaux-Arts' in Paris, and he designed 'the pedestal of the Statue of Liberty' and Biltmore, 'America's largest private house'. [short pause] For Chicago's richest man he built a broad brick and stone mansion under a mansard; it ends as an aeronautical university and is razed in 1955. [short pause] One more stop, at 2100, where a young architect met his wife.
scripts.stop:sherman: [measured] 2100 Prairie, John B. Sherman's house of 1874, the first of nearly a dozen Burnham and Root commissions on this street. [short pause] Sherman ran the Union Stock Yards. While the house was going up, his daughter Margaret married the young architect Daniel Burnham, in 1876, and Sherman started telling his neighbours whom to hire. [short pause] That is how a firm gets a street: the client becomes your father-in-law, and the father-in-law becomes your salesman. Burnham and Root became the most prolific architects on Prairie Avenue. [short pause] The house where it started is razed in 1936.
scripts.ending:finish:
[measured] End of the walk at 2100 Prairie. These seven houses are a sketchbook of the architects who rebuilt Chicago after the fire. [short pause] A few years from now Burnham will take the lesson from this street to the whole city: his 1909 Plan of Chicago, 'the first comprehensive plan for the controlled growth of an American city'.

[short pause] Look for their other fronts as you explore. Every one of them is signed in stone.
